entries.title: Another Federal Judge Declines to Block Trump’s Taxpayer-Funded Ads After DNC Lawsuit
entries.summary: Government lawyers argued at a hearing last week that the court should not issue orders pausing the ads to address “past harm.”
entries.content:
A federal judge on Wednesday declined to block the Trump administration from spending taxpayer dollars on campaign-style advertisements, rejecting the Democratic National Committee’s request for a continued pause on airing ads funded with public money.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan ruled the DNC had failed to demonstrate irreparable harm in a legal battle over White House advertisements that began airing weeks before the midterm elections. Critics have dubbed the spots “propaganda,” with several ads featuring stylized edits of the president and Cabinet officials, Republican rhetoric on the dangers of communism and U.S. missile strikes on Iran.

The ads are facing three separate legal challenges. The lawsuit the DNC brought is notable because the committee alleges the government unlawfully used public funds to develop and produce the ads, while the other cases primarily take issue with the government paying for their being broadcast.

Before AliKhan’s initial temporary restraining order — which blocked the administration from using taxpayer funds to create and air the ads — expired, the DNC urged the court to indefinitely keep those restrictions in place until the court handed down a final decision

During a hearing last Thursday, AliKhan mulled over how to view the facts of the case and whether the ads presented irreparable harm to the DNC in a post-midterm elections context.

“The next relevant election is two years away,” Justice Department attorney Elisabeth Neylan told the court, adding that the court should not issue longer-lasting restrictions on the ads to remedy “past harm.”

DNC attorney Daniel Freeman acknowledged that the harm may have been greater near the “end of October, but that doesn’t mean that it goes away entirely.” Freeman said the court cannot ignore that the ads undermine Democrats’ chances in both immediate and future elections — including U.S. House runoff elections in Louisiana this December, Minnesota’s U.S. Senate race in 2027 and the 2028 elections.

“The unique position of the DNC is that we are supporting candidates up and down the ticket in all 50 states,” Freeman said, arguing that the imminent harm does not just exist for the larger contests in the next two years.

Freeman also said that many of President Donald Trump’s “self-aggrandizing” ads do not have “anything to do with policy at all” and constitute clear propaganda — which government staffers are expressly prohibited from creating and distributing.

The administration’s attorney did not officially take a position on whether the ads are propaganda, but she argued that “under plaintiff’s theory, this court would wade into” every speech or Truth Social post written by White House staffers for Trump.

AliKhan expressed concerns about becoming a “content editor for the White House” in this case, adding that she worried about returning to court “every time a new YouTube ad drops.”

The DNC argued in court filings that White House employees’ alleged involvement in the ads represents a violation of federal law meant to prevent political staff from performing campaign-related work. Reports indicate that the administration developed at least a dozen ads, but only several aired with a disclaimer reading “Paid for by the U.S. Government” before the courts intervened.

Wednesday’s order follows another federal judge’s decision last week in a separate case not to extend restrictions on ads. In that case, U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon ruled that the arguments from the plaintiffs who brought the suit were “too speculative and non-imminent” to justify continued emergency relief — while allowing the case to proceed on the legal questions surrounding the administration’s use of taxpayer funds to cut the ads.

The Office of Management and Budget earlier this year reallocated $20 million in One Big Beautiful Bill Act funding within U.S. Customs and Border Protection for “commemorative events.” The Department of Homeland Security subsequently entered into a $19 million media buy contract with LMD Agency to air the ads.

Facing scrutiny from both Democrats and Republican lawmakers, Trump announced in an Oct. 5 post on Truth Social that he planned to “pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.” — a move that may violate federal campaign-finance laws that prohibit a president from directing spending decisions for a super PAC. The White House confirmed that Trump did not plan to reimburse the federal government for taxpayer funds already used for the ads.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Court Halts FCC From Threatening ABC Stations’ Broadcast Licenses
entries.summary: The judge called the lawsuit “not a close case” and found ABC was likely to prove the FCC retaliated against the broadcaster for speech critical of the president.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Wednesday halted early license-renewal proceedings for eight ABC-owned stations that began a day after President Donald Trump demanded the network fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel.

In a scathing 45-page opinion issued Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan noted how quickly the Federal Communications Commission acted after Trump demanded ABC and its parent, The Walt Disney Company, fire Kimmel over a joke about first lady Melania Trump. The FCC ordered the stations in April to apply for broadcast license renewal, years before their licenses were set to expire.

“Chairman Carr has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders” AliKhan wrote, referencing FCC Chair Brendan Carr. “Against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr’s call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings.”

The preliminary injunction pauses the renewal proceedings for eight ABC-owned stations while their suit against the FCC continues.

In her ruling, AliKhan found that ABC was likely to prove the FCC acted in retaliation against the broadcaster’s protected speech.

“This is not a close case,” the judge wrote. “Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.”
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: The Caps Snap Their Losing Streak With a 7-3 Win Over Flyers
entries.summary: Washington scored four times inside the final three minutes.
entries.content:
Alex Tuch had a goal and two assists, and the Washington Capitals scored four times inside the final three minutes of a 7-3 victory over the Philadelphia Flyers on Wednesday night.

Ryan Leonard scored his 10th goal and added his ninth assist as Washington snapped a five-game slide and improved to 5-1-0 at home against Metropolitan Division opponents.

Matt Roy and Ivan Miroshnichenko also contributed to the late onslaught and picked up assists, and Dylan Strome had the final Washington goal with 11 seconds remaining.

Earlier, Cole Hutson scored Washington’s sixth power-play goal in many games to put Washington ahead for good midway through the second period. Boone Jenner made it 3-1 before the end of the third period after Ilya Protas poked the puck away from goaltender Joseph Woll near his own goal.

Logan Thompson made 18 saves to preserve his first regulation victory since a 4-3 win over Florida on Nov. 7.

Travis Konecny gave the Flyers the lead 17 seconds into the game and later assisted on Rasmus Ristolainen's goal 1:59 into the third that cut the deficit to 3-2. Cole Knuble added a late consolation goal as Philadelphia saw its three-game win streak snapped and failed to earn a road point for the first time in seven games.

Woll stopped 28 of 34 shots for the Flyers.

The Capitals honored Alex Ovechkin in a pregame ceremony for becoming the team's career assists leader with his 763rd last Thursday against Buffalo. The seven-minute presentation included a video message from retired Caps player Nicklas Backstrom, whom Ovechkin passed.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: A Chief Architect of the Clean Water Act Thinks Permitting Reform Is Missing the Point
entries.summary: Permitting takes too long. But Tom Jorling says the Clean Water Act isn’t the issue.
entries.content:
As a kid in Cincinnati, Tom Jorling’s parents told him to stay away from the Ohio River. These days, he says, the same water that was too contaminated to touch is filled with luxury boats.

“Now I go back there, and you think you’re in Nantucket,” he said.

Jorling helped write the laws that made that happen, drafting the Clean Air Act and the Clean Water Act as counsel for Republicans on the Senate Public Works Committee in the 1970s. Those years were intense, he said, but unusually collaborative and productive, with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle backing major policy change.

This year, another group of lawmakers is pushing forward a similarly transformative, bipartisan bill: an effort to revise bedrock environmental laws, including the Clean Water Act, to reform the permitting system. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which passed in the Senate last week and now faces a fight in the House, is meant to speed up energy projects by reducing red tape.

Jorling says those pushing the bill forward are leaving behind decades of progress.

“They’re turning a blind eye to the success that [the Clean Water Act] had, and then trying to claim that the provisions of these successful laws are preventing things, which I don’t believe they are,” he said.

Proponents of permitting reform say it takes too long to build energy projects. On the left, lawmakers are thinking about the solar, wind and batteries that could help transition the grid away from climate-warming fossil fuels and the power lines that could carry that electricity across the country. On the right, wins for gas pipelines, power plants and mines are fueling support, along with the Trump administration’s push for “energy dominance.” Affordability concerns have allowed legislators to unite forces.

Jorling is sympathetic to the idea of permitting reform. After helping to create the Clean Water Act, he joined the Environmental Protection Agency and later led New York’s Department of Environmental Conservation. He also worked in the private sector in environmental affairs at International Paper.

He said he saw firsthand how “bureaucracies can gum up the process.” He said he would support permitting reform that required decisions to be made more quickly. But changing federal environmental regulations, he said, would be more ideological than effective, especially because so much permitting happens at the state and local levels.

“It’s the local permitting and approvals that are the problem, and they’re using the guise of the federal government to try and put limitations on those state bodies or local government bodies in order to bypass them,” he said. “I’m not sure how that’s consistent with old-time Republican or conservative orthodoxy.”

The bill would make changes to a host of environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act. The section changing the Clean Water Act has concerned some Democrats, who say it could degrade the environmental gains of the past five decades.

The Clean Water Act made it illegal to discharge pollution into waters without a permit. The law also requires states, territories and tribes to maintain water quality standards. Under the Clean Water Act, citizens can sue polluters or the EPA for failing to carry out their responsibilities under the law.

The permitting reform bill would establish firm timelines for reviews that apply to infrastructure running across bodies of water. It would also limit states and tribes to only consider water quality issues spelled out in the law when issuing Clean Water Act certifications. Transmission lines and gas pipelines would only need reviews of specific pollution discharge points, not the full range of the project.

Jorling said during the development of the Clean Water Act, lawmakers wanted to protect states’ authority in the permitting process and ensure that the federal government didn’t override that authority. The law allows states to set more restrictive standards than the federal government.

Jorling said provisions protecting states’ rights were “strongly advocated by Republicans.”

“Now to hear Republicans basically trying to limit or control the states’ rights is quite surprising,” he said.

The permitting bill also would double the amount of time pollution discharge permits are valid, from five years to 10 years. Jorling called that “unnecessary,” saying the reason for the five-year term was to encourage periodic upgrades as technology improves.

“It’s another effort to lock in substandard performance,” he said. “I just find that sort of baffling, because industry always says, ‘Well, we want to do the best we can with the best technology.’”

The bill would also create a 150-day statute of limitations for lawsuits that have to do with pollution from dredging or filling wetlands or water bodies, and limit lawsuits so they can only be filed by those who have commented on a project during the public comment period on the issue they are suing over.

Jorling said the change seemed like an effort to protect the EPA from legal issues.

“I'm suspicious that they're trying a backdoor way of relaxing the requirements,” he said.

The permitting bill’s sponsors have defended its provisions, saying the changes to the Clean Water Act are common-sense solutions to the ways that law can get in the way of development, and won’t gut environmental protections.

“Gas pipelines and transmission lines have both fallen victim to state politics on occasion,” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) said in a floor speech on the bill. “The changes in this subsection are designed to focus states on the Clean Water Act essential: ensuring water quality.”

But some Democrats have pushed back on the Clean Water Act changes. Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vermont) voted against the bill, saying one of his concerns was its effect on clean water resources. He filed amendments that were not included in the bill that would have protected states’ abilities to consider a wider range of effects to water.

In the House, Rep. Maxine Waters (D-California) noted her concern over the way the Clean Water Act provisions could limit communities’ ability to challenge projects or provide input. Rep. Mike Levin (D-California) said the bill would limit California’s ability to protect its water.

Whitehouse has said the bill would help push the clean energy transition forward, paving the way for more renewables moving more quickly onto the grid. But when it comes to the Clean Water Act provisions, Jorling said he didn’t know of any renewable energy projects that required a Clean Water Act permit and called the argument that law holds renewable energy back a “political ploy.”

“I don’t think the Clean Water Act is much of a barrier,” he said.

entries.title: Thanksgiving Day Storm Slams D.C. With Strong Winds
entries.summary: Flight cancellations and power outages are climbing with strong wind gusts and heavy rain hitting the East Coast.
entries.content:
A severe storm on Thanksgiving is bringing powerful winds, heavy rain and possible flash flooding across the mid-Atlantic and Northeast, disrupting travel during the holiday.

The National Weather Service has issued high winds and storm warnings from Virginia Beach to southern New England, and the Washington, D.C., region is seeing strong wind gusts of 40 to 60 miles per hour, according to Capital Weather.

D.C. is expected to get over 2 inches of rain, with gusty winds forecasted to last until 7 p.m. Thursday, and a coastal flood warning in effect until 3 a.m. Friday. NWS is warning that downed trees and heavy rain could make driving conditions in D.C. dangerous.

The Maryland Transportation Authority temporarily closed the Chesapeake Bay Bridge late Thursday morning because of strong winds, according to a post on X.

Already more than 207,000 people in Virginia have lost power, mostly around the coast. Nearly 74,000 people are without power in Maryland and 775 in D.C., according to poweroutage.com.

As of late morning, approximately 400 flights have been canceled and more than 1,000 have been delayed, according to FlightAware, snarling busy holiday travel. In the DMV, 20% of the flights departing from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport have been delayed and 10% canceled. At the Baltimore-Washington International Airport, 26% of flights have been canceled and 12% have been delayed.

Ahead of the storm’s arrival, the milestone 100th annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade was postponed to Saturday. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the decision was made “out of an abundance of caution.” The decision marks the first time the parade has been delayed due to weather.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill issued a statewide state of emergency Wednesday night and urged people against driving on flooded roads. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City and Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties Wednesday night.
entries.author: Jackie Llanos
